gist: Harley Bassman tells Dean Curnutt the long-end US yield backup is a fiscal trust problem (not inflation), amplified by rate-insensitive supply from the US government and AI hyperscalers (~$2.7T combined), and expects debasement over default. He favors 2-year Treasuries near 5% and cheap TIPS real yields, views MOVE at 100 as a return to its 1990s norm, and says equities stay supported by passive flows until unemployment nears 5%.

themes.theme: Fiscal trust premium driving long-end yields

insights.claim: Harley Bassman argues the backup in US long-end yields is a trust problem, not an inflation problem: 10-year breakevens have hovered around 2.35% for four years while rates rose about 150bp, so the move reflects distrust of US fiscal control and the dollar.
insights.speaker: Harley Bassman
insights.so_what: Long-end selloff is a term/credibility premium story, so inflation prints alone won't reverse it.
insights.quote: we don't have an inflation problem with rates going higher. We have a trust problem.

insights.claim: Bassman attributes the rate backup as 95% fiscal: the US has roughly $5 trillion of income vs $7 trillion of expenses, interest costs are about $1.1-1.2 trillion, and at $40 trillion of debt marked at 5% interest would approach $2 trillion once low-coupon debt rolls off, exceeding defense spending.
insights.speaker: Harley Bassman
insights.so_what: Interest-cost compounding makes the fiscal path self-reinforcing and keeps term premium elevated.
insights.quote: It is a 95% fiscal problem.

insights.claim: Bassman notes a roughly 6% fiscal deficit (~$2 trillion) with ~4.2% unemployment and the S&P near highs is unprecedented outside of war or recession.
insights.speaker: Harley Bassman
insights.so_what: Deficits are pro-cyclical at full employment, leaving no fiscal room for the next downturn.
insights.quote: it's unprecedented to have a 6% fiscal deficit without being at war or being in a recession.

insights.claim: Bassman believes the US will inflate its way out of the debt rather than default or grow out, making inflation a silent bipartisan tax on the middle class and implying currency debasement; he likes gold and real estate and sees owning paper money as tough.
insights.speaker: Harley Bassman
insights.so_what: Favors real assets and pricing-power equities over nominal dollar claims over the long run.
insights.quote: Inflation is the only tax that both Republicans and Democrats can agree on because you never vote on it.

insights.claim: Bassman says the US dollar will likely follow Japan's path, where the yen moved from 80 to 160 as the escape valve for a 200-300% debt-to-GDP ratio, though he is unsure what the dollar will fall against since Western Europe and Japan are no better.
insights.speaker: Harley Bassman
insights.so_what: Currency debasement rather than default is the release valve; relative-value FX views are hard since all fiat is debasing.
insights.quote: the US dollar will go down the same path I suppose at some point I'm not sure versus what

insights.claim: Bassman dismisses Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's buyback talk and the Trump-directed $200 billion Fannie/Freddie mortgage purchases as non-plans: buybacks are too small relative to $40 trillion of debt and mortgage spreads tightened only a dime for a week or two before giving it back.
insights.speaker: Harley Bassman
insights.so_what: Don't fade long-end weakness on official jawboning or small-scale buybacks; effects are transient.
insights.quote: These aren't plans. They're like, I don't know, short-term coin flips.

insights.claim: Bassman says what would bring rates down is an agreed credible path to fiscal control (like Clinton-era Social Security fixes or Simpson-Bowles), not an immediate solution; he expects measures like uncapping the Social Security wage base from $184,000, means-testing Social Security/Medicare and ending step-up basis, while calling a wealth tax meaningless.
insights.speaker: Harley Bassman
insights.so_what: Watch for a credible fiscal framework as the catalyst for long-end rally; step-up basis repeal would matter for estate/asset holders.
insights.quote: All we need is a path that's agreed upon that we're going to go and start down and do something.

insights.claim: Bassman warns of an eventual US debt spiral if $2 trillion annual deficits continue without controls, but says it could take 20 years, so investors should not short the market yet.
insights.speaker: Harley Bassman
insights.so_what: Long-horizon tail risk, not a near-term trade trigger.
insights.quote: it could take 20 years for this to happen. So, so don't don't go short yet the market yet

insights.claim: Bassman sees term limits as the number one solution to the fiscal problem because politicians rationally kick the can to get re-elected, and calls MMT a false god since politicians cannot cut spending or raise taxes when inflation appears.
insights.speaker: Harley Bassman
insights.so_what: Structural political incentives argue the fiscal premium is persistent absent institutional change.
insights.quote: term limits would be this the the number one solution to this whole thing.

themes.theme: Rate-insensitive supply: hyperscalers and the government

insights.claim: Bassman frames the long-end selloff as a supply issue rather than a buyer-base change: about $2 trillion of new US government debt this year (about $4 trillion including rollovers) plus roughly $750 billion of hyperscaler borrowing from five big companies, about a third on top of government issuance.
insights.speaker: Harley Bassman
insights.so_what: AI capex debt competes directly with Treasuries for duration buyers, pressuring 10s and 30s.
insights.quote: I think it's the supply. It's just there's a fiscal situation out of control with the hyperscalers.

insights.claim: Bassman argues hyperscalers are totally rate-insensitive borrowers because the AI race is existential and only one or two of the five will survive, so they will issue at 6, 8, 10 or 12%; if Oracle goes from 6 to 8 or Meta from 7 to 9 it does not matter.
insights.speaker: Harley Bassman
insights.so_what: Higher rates won't throttle AI capex issuance, so 'cure for high rates is high rates' fails in bonds.
insights.quote: They can borrow at 6, 8, 10, 12. It just doesn't matter because these five guys know only one or two of them are going to live, right?

insights.claim: Bassman thinks hyperscaler bonds are probably money good because all five issuers have cash-producing core businesses to cover coupons and likely principal, while equity holders may take the hit if they lose the AI race.
insights.speaker: Harley Bassman
insights.so_what: Prefer hyperscaler credit over equity for AI-capex exposure; losers' equity bears the risk.
insights.quote: The equity guy now, he might take a hit. Okay. But the bond guy, I I I I think you know, you're you're probably money good

insights.claim: Bassman says the two biggest borrowers, the US government and hyperscalers (about $2.7 trillion combined), are price-insensitive, so higher rates hurt credit cards, auto and mortgages but don't curb the dominant demand for credit.
insights.speaker: Harley Bassman
insights.so_what: Rate hikes transmit unevenly: consumer/housing sectors bear the pain while aggregate borrowing continues.
insights.quote: we have the two biggest borrowers basically $2.7 trillion who are totally price insensitive

insights.claim: Bassman notes non-bank private credit has stepped into the banks' shoes and is not beholden to the Fed, weakening monetary transmission; he doubts moving the policy rate by 100bp affects the economy at all.
insights.speaker: Harley Bassman
insights.so_what: Fed tightening may have muted macro effect, lengthening the period of elevated rates.
insights.quote: I don't think moving rates up or down by 100 impacts the economy at all

insights.claim: Bassman expects less foreign demand for Treasuries: Japanese life companies and investors no longer find USD-JPY rate spreads attractive after hedging costs, and pensions and insurers, now fully funded, have largely defeased and are running out of gas as 30-year buyers.
insights.speaker: Harley Bassman
insights.so_what: Marginal long-end buyers are shrinking, adding to term premium.
insights.quote: who buys a 30-year bond? Nobody.

insights.claim: Bassman explains gold's recent decline (still around $4,000, well above two years ago) as a function of rising rates and margin-call liquidation, while foreigners shift from Western paper into gold and stocks.
insights.speaker: Harley Bassman
insights.so_what: Gold pullback may be forced selling rather than a thesis break.
insights.quote: when you when you get margin called, man, you you sell what you can, not what you uh not what you want to.

themes.theme: Fed policy, forward guidance and moral hazard

insights.claim: Bassman's last two commentaries argued Fed Chair Warsh should hike 50bp one-and-done to prove independence from President Trump, since cutting now would make him look like a sycophant; he says Warsh didn't have the votes.
insights.speaker: Harley Bassman
insights.so_what: Fed credibility signaling, not data, may drive near-term policy surprises.
insights.quote: Hike 50, one and done.

insights.claim: Bassman argues forward guidance and dots create moral hazard, citing Greenspan's 2004 'measured pace' (hedge funds selling 27bp out-of-the-money puts and levering up into 2006-08) and the Fed's 2021-22 zero-rate guidance that led Silicon Valley Bank to buy unhedged long duration.
insights.speaker: Harley Bassman
insights.so_what: Explicit guidance breeds crowded leverage; watch for blowups where positioning relied on Fed promises.
insights.quote: I don't like dots. I don't like forward guidance. All those things do is create moral hazard.

insights.claim: Bassman now views the oil shock as transitory because oil is not sensitive to the Fed's rate and will come down when the war ends, unlike his rejection of 'transitory' several years ago.
insights.speaker: Harley Bassman
insights.so_what: Oil-driven inflation shouldn't justify a sustained hiking cycle.
insights.quote: I never believed in the word transitory, you know, three, four, five years ago. I kind of believe in it now because oil is a transitory cost.

insights.claim: Bassman notes US corporate net interest income/expense (citing Albert Edwards) is near zero or positive, so raising short rates may actually boost the economy by paying cash-rich boomers and corporations; host Dean Curnutt adds Warren Buffett holds about $380 billion of short Treasuries.
insights.speaker: Harley Bassman
insights.so_what: Higher policy rates may be stimulative via interest income, undermining the tightening channel.
insights.quote: taking rates up actually increases the economy.

insights.claim: Bassman calls the Fed boxed in: hiking worsens home affordability and government interest costs, cutting inflames inflation fears and the back end; he said QE beyond QE1 was never a good idea.
insights.speaker: Harley Bassman
insights.so_what: No clean policy exit implies continued rate volatility.
insights.quote: The Fed's in a box.

themes.theme: Positioning: front end, TIPS and real rates

insights.claim: Bassman calls two-year US Treasuries near 5% the best trade in the market: almost no duration risk and a state-and-local-tax-free yield.
insights.speaker: Harley Bassman
insights.so_what: Front-end Treasuries offer an attractive risk-adjusted carry with upside if growth cracks.
insights.quote: The best trade in the market right now, I'm I'm sorry, call it trade is probably two-year US treasuries up to 5%.

insights.claim: Bassman says real yields of about 2.5-3% on TIPS across 5s, 10s and 30s are crazy cheap, provided CPI reflects real inflation, because large holders have nowhere else to store money safely without default risk.
insights.speaker: Harley Bassman
insights.so_what: Locking in high default-free real rates is attractive for large capital pools.
insights.quote: I think it's crazy cheap.

insights.claim: Bassman suggests rising real yields may reflect a market belief that CPI understates true inflation, since the late-1990s changes (hedonics, substitution, quality adjustments) were designed to keep CPI and indexed benefits low.
insights.speaker: Harley Bassman
insights.so_what: Breakevens may understate inflation risk; real-world inflation hits median households harder.
insights.quote: What's wrong with this picture might be that CPI is cooked.

insights.claim: Bassman says the forward one-year rate one year out implied about 2.5% earlier this year when three cuts were priced, which he shorted as insane, but now both the rate surface and vol surface are dead flat, offering nothing.
insights.speaker: Harley Bassman
insights.so_what: Curve-based trades currently lack edge; wait for distortions.
insights.quote: A forward rate is not a prediction. It's the market's break even.

insights.claim: In an equity selloff with unemployment at 5% and VIX at 30, Bassman expects a massive bull steepener: two-year yields falling perhaps 50-100bp with the long end moving less; using fed funds at about 3.90% plus a 50bp spread, fair value for 2s is around 4.40% versus about 4.90% trading.
insights.speaker: Harley Bassman
insights.so_what: Front end is the best hedge for risk-off; position for steepeners on growth shocks.
insights.quote: Yes, you have a bull steepening.

themes.theme: MOVE index and volatility as a trading tool

insights.claim: Bassman explains the MOVE index (created in 1994 with data back to 1988) is a real implied-volatility number: a MOVE of 100 implies 10-year yields within ±100bp a year out 68% of the time (about 6bp per day); it weights 20% 2s, 20% 5s, 40% 10s and 20% 30s.
insights.speaker: Harley Bassman
insights.so_what: Divide implied vol by 16 for expected daily moves to judge whether options are rich or cheap.
insights.quote: If you took stat 9th grade, you could be a professional option trader.

insights.claim: Bassman says a MOVE above 100 is not elevated historically: it averaged 100 through the 1990s, and the low readings of the QE era were artificial; his 1990s rule was buy 80, sell 120.
insights.speaker: Harley Bassman
insights.so_what: Today's rate vol is a normalization, not a crisis signal; 5% tens are 'back to the future'.
insights.quote: My rule of thumb in the 90s was buy 80, sell 120.

insights.claim: Bassman notes 2-year Treasury implied vol (~115) currently exceeds long-bond vol (~85), the reverse of QE periods when the Fed suppressed the front end.
insights.speaker: Harley Bassman
insights.so_what: Front-end policy uncertainty is now the dominant rate risk.
insights.quote: Right now you have twos at 115 and and and bonds at 85.

insights.claim: Bassman sold strangles on silver when its implied volatility hit about 120, judging the implied daily move unsustainable.
insights.speaker: Harley Bassman
insights.so_what: Example of selling extreme commodity vol using the divide-by-16 rule.

themes.theme: Equities: passive flows and K-shaped economy

insights.claim: Bassman, citing Michael Green, argues passive 401k flows drive US equities with no value construct, and because megacaps like Apple are less liquid than their weight implies, inflows push them disproportionately higher (and outflows will do the reverse).
insights.speaker: Harley Bassman
insights.so_what: Megacap concentration is flow-driven and will reverse violently when flows turn.
insights.quote: There's no value construct.

insights.claim: Bassman says the trigger for equity selling is unemployment rising to roughly 4.5-5%+, which would stop 401k contributions while boomers make mandatory withdrawals; until then, he does not see a hard break in stocks.
insights.speaker: Harley Bassman
insights.so_what: Watch the unemployment rate, not valuations, as the equity risk trigger.
insights.quote: What will cause selling is the question then. Well, the answer is unemployment over 5%.

insights.claim: Bassman says stocks are holding up because equities represent businesses that can raise prices with inflation, citing Weimar Germany where held stocks preserved value.
insights.speaker: Harley Bassman
insights.so_what: Pricing-power equities are an inflation/debasement hedge.
insights.quote: one of the best hedges against inflation is owning a stock that can raise their price and manage their business.

insights.claim: Bassman says if one wanted to hedge, S&P out-of-the-money puts are cheap because rates above the dividend yield push the S&P forward higher, making a 10% OTM put effectively 12-14% OTM, though he is not recommending it; rates hitting 6% could eventually pressure stocks.
insights.speaker: Harley Bassman
insights.so_what: Positive carry makes downside puts and collars structurally cheaper now.
insights.quote: S&P out of the money puts are probably your best hedge.

insights.claim: Bassman describes a K-shaped economy where mean statistics mask median pain: incomes roughly doubled over 30-40 years while housing, health care and college rose 4-5x; housing affordability is below 100, and the median household cannot buy the median home with 30-year mortgages around 7.2%.
insights.speaker: Harley Bassman
insights.so_what: Aggregate spending is propped up by the top decile; housing-linked and median-consumer sectors are vulnerable.
insights.quote: your median person can't buy your median house.
